content: 1. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and aromatase inhibitors are pharmacological agents that act by reducing estrogen levels in the body. 2. Other pharmacological interventions include drugs aimed at reversing insulin resistance, such as metformin, or medications designed to promote weight loss, including appetite suppressants or agents that reduce fat absorption. 3. Non-pharmacological interventions, such as lifestyle modifications, focus on promoting weight loss through dietary changes to reduce nutrient intake and increasing physical activity. 4. These lifestyle interventions, while beneficial, are unlikely to produce rapid effects in the context of untreated cancer and are therefore beyond the scope of this Cochrane Review. 5. Weight loss interventions for women undergoing conventional treatment for endometrial cancer have been reviewed in other studies, such as Kitson (2018). 6. Bariatric surgery, also known as weight loss surgery, is a treatment for morbid obesity and is the only intervention proven to achieve sustained weight loss over the long term (Khwaja 2010). 7. In addition to weight reduction, bariatric surgery is associated with significant improvement or even resolution of obesity-related comorbidities, including Type II diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnea, hypertension, asthma, osteoarthritis, cancer risk, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (Adams 2009; Upala 2015). 8. Common bariatric techniques include Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, adjustable gastric banding, and sleeve gastrectomy, typically performed via laparoscopic approaches. 9. Bariatric surgery may also be considered as part of primary prevention strategies for endometrial cancer, although data on its use as a treatment for established cancer remain limited. 10. Obesity is a major risk factor for endometrial cancer and hyperplasia, with a recent meta-analysis showing that the risk of endometrial cancer increases with rising body weight (Jenabi 2015). 11. In obese women, a metabolic state characterized by hyperestrogenemia, inflammation, and insulin resistance promotes oncogenesis by altering oncogenic signaling pathways (Mackintosh 2013). 12. Excess endogenous estrogens produced by adipose tissue in obese women or chronic anovulation are common causes of hyperestrogenemia. 13. Hormonal treatments aim to counteract the effects of estrogens or reduce estrogen levels. 14. Progesterone is the most widely used hormonal treatment, but GnRH agonists and aromatase inhibitors have also been employed. 15. Progesterone plays a critical role in limiting the proliferative effects of estrogens on the endometrium. 16. Progestins exhibit additional anti-proliferative effects, including inhibition of estrogen receptors, anti-angiogenic actions, and suppression of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) (Kim 2013). 17. Endometrial hyperplasia expresses high levels of progesterone receptors (Miyamoto 2004). 18. Low-grade endometrial cancer often expresses both estrogen and progesterone receptors (PR) (Darvishian 2004; Demopoulos 1999). 19. Tumors that are PR-negative do not respond to progestin treatment, although PR expression alone does not guarantee a sustained response, as less than half of women demonstrate long-term efficacy. 20. Studies on progesterone treatment for endometrial cancer report complete response rates ranging from 48% to 87% and recurrence rates between 20% and 47% (Erkanli 2010; Gallos 2012; Gunderson 2012; Ushijima 2007; Wei 2017). 21. GnRH agonists reduce estrogen levels by suppressing the release of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). 22. Aromatase inhibitors block estrogen production in peripheral adipose tissue. 23. Insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia are key contributors to endometrial hyperplasia and may play a role in the initiation of endometrial cancer (Shan 2014). 24. Interventions targeting insulin resistance include both pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches, such as weight-loss surgery. 25. Metformin, an anti-diabetic drug, regulates glucose metabolism and has multiple anti-proliferative mechanisms, including reducing insulin and IGF-1 levels (Ferguson 2013; Kim 2013; Wang 2012), increasing progesterone receptor expression, and reducing progesterone resistance (Xie 2011). 26. A meta-analysis suggests that metformin is effective in reversing proliferation biomarkers associated with tumor progression and may lead to the reversal of atypical hyperplasia or improved survival in endometrial cancer (Meireles 2017). 27. Weight loss interventions, including lifestyle changes, in obese women at risk of endometrial cancer can alter blood biomarkers associated with the disease (Yates 2017). 28. Breast cancer, like endometrial cancer, can be hormonally driven. 29. In breast cancer, weight loss interventions reduce total and free estradiol levels (Rock 2013). 30. These interventions, either alone or in combination with metformin (Patterson 2018), can reduce recurrence and mortality rates. 31. A meta-analysis evaluating the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and mortality in endometrial cancer found that increased BMI is associated with higher mortality (Secord 2016). 32. Weight-loss interventions may improve survival in women with endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia by targeting pathways linking obesity and endometrial cancer. 33. Observational evidence links intentional surgical weight loss with reductions in endometrial cancer incidence (Anveden 2017; Luo).
